title: En passant: the chess capture that looks like a mistake
description: Your pawn is standing still — and your opponent captures it anyway, landing on a square your pawn never occupied. En passant is chess's strangest rule: a capture of a pawn that has just sprinted past you, allowed for exactly one move.

body.heading: The sprint that created the rule
paragraphs: Centuries ago, pawns could only ever move one square at a time, so an enemy pawn waiting beside your pawn could always capture it as it crept past. When the rules were sped up to let a pawn dash two squares on its first move, a pawn could suddenly sprint straight past an enemy pawn that would once have caught it — and that felt like cheating.

En passant, French for 'in passing', is the patch. If your pawn sits on its fifth rank and an enemy pawn dashes two squares to land beside it, you may capture it exactly as if it had moved only one square. Your pawn lands on the square the enemy pawn passed through, and the sprinting pawn comes off the board.

body.heading: One move only — or never
paragraphs: The catch is the deadline. The en passant capture is legal only on the very next move, immediately after the two-square dash. Hesitate for even one turn, play anything else first, and the chance is gone forever, however unfair that feels.

It is also the only capture in chess where the capturing piece does not land on the captured piece's square — which is why it looks like a bug the first time someone does it to you. It is not. It is one of the oldest special rules in the game, and forgetting it has decided real tournament games.

body.heading: Spot it before it spots you
paragraphs: Train your eye with one habit: whenever an enemy pawn makes its first move, glance at where it lands. If it has come to rest beside one of your advanced pawns, you are holding a one-move ticket — use it or lose it.
And when you are the one tempted to dash a pawn two squares to escape danger, check the neighbouring files first. The square you sprint past may be exactly where your pawn gets caught.

takeaway: En passant lets you capture a pawn that has just dashed two squares past yours — as if it had moved one — but only on the very next move.
